A room can feel incredibly stuffy even at a comfortable temperature due to high humidity and a lack of airflow. 

When relative humidity is high, the air is saturated with moisture. This slows down the rate at which sweat evaporates from your skin, preventing your body's natural cooling process and making the air feel thick and heavy. 

Without active airflow, this stagnant air traps heat, moisture, and carbon dioxide in a localized "envelope" around your body. Without a breeze or ventilation to disperse these elements, the air becomes stale. Essentially, stagnant, moisture-laden air prevents your skin from breathing, turning a thermally comfortable room into a suffocating environment.

A room can feel stuffy even at a comfortable temperature because comfort depends on more than heat. Humidity matters: when the air holds a lot of moisture, sweat evaporates from your skin more slowly, so the air feels heavy, sticky, and close. Airflow matters too. In still air, a thin layer of warm, moist air tends to cling around your body, and without a breeze to carry it away, the space feels stagnant. Poor ventilation can also let cooking smells, dust, and other odors linger, reinforcing that "used air" impression. Opening a window, running a fan, or using a dehumidifier or exhaust vent often makes the room feel fresher without changing the temperature.
task: Explain why a room can feel stuffy even when the temperature is comfortable. Discuss humidity and airflow without giving medical advice.

text: This classroom project evaluated the structural stability of three common cardboard bridge designs: flat, arch, and pleated accordion folds. Using corrugated cardboard sheets of identical dimensions, we constructed simplified model spans of 30 centimeters. We progressively applied localized weights to the center of each span until structural failure occurred, recording the maximum load endured. Due to the small sample size and manual construction variations, these findings are highly preliminary. While the accordion-fold design withstood the highest average weight, these results are limited to our specific classroom materials. They illustrate basic engineering principles but cannot be used to predict the behavior of real-world load-bearing structures.

This fictional classroom project compared the stability of three folded cardboard bridge designs: flat, accordion-folded, and triangular-truss. Each bridge was built from identical sheets of corrugated cardboard and spanned a 30-centimeter gap between two desks. Students added coins one at a time to the center of each bridge until it sagged visibly or collapsed, repeating each trial three times. The project's scope was limited by a small number of trials, inconsistent folding by hand, and the use of a single material and span length. In these trials, the folded designs appeared to hold more coins than the flat design. However, these results should be viewed as a simple classroom demonstration rather than reliable scientific evidence.
